summary: Susanna, the godly wife of Joakim, is spied on by two elders who serve as judges. When she refuses them, they accuse her of adultery with a fictitious lover — and the assembly, believing the judges, condemns her to death. As she is led away, the young Daniel, stirred by the Holy Spirit, cries 'I am clear from the blood of this woman,' separates the two witnesses, and breaks their story on the detail of a tree: one swears it happened under a mastic, the other under a holm oak. The innocent blood is saved; the false judges die by the law they twisted.
whyItMatters: This is the Bible's great courtroom drama about due process — and its first sustained portrait of cross-examination. 'Without examination or knowledge of the truth ye have condemned' (13:48) is a principle every legal system since has had to reckon with. It is also one of Scripture's clearest stories of a woman choosing death over sin.

context.author: Unknown; composed in Greek (possibly translated from a Semitic original), appended to Daniel
context.audience: Jewish readers in the Greek period; beloved in the early church
context.date: Likely 2nd-1st century BC in its Greek form; set in Babylon during the exile
context.setting: Babylon — Joakim's house and garden, and the public assembly

keyVerses.text: I am straitened on every side: for if I do this thing, it is death to me: and if I do it not, I shall not escape your hands. But it is better for me to fall into your hands without doing it, than to sin in the sight of the Lord.
keyVerses.why: The moral summit of the chapter — trapped between two deaths, Susanna chooses the one that keeps her conscience clean.

keyVerses.text: O eternal God, who knowest hidden things, who knowest all things before they come to pass: thou knowest that they have borne false witness against me.
keyVerses.why: Her appeal is to the only witness who was actually in the garden — the God who sees what is hidden.

keyVerses.text: Are ye so foolish, ye children of Israel, that without examination or knowledge of the truth, you have condemned a daughter of Israel?
keyVerses.why: Daniel's rebuke is procedural, not just moral: condemnation without examination is folly — the seed of every later standard of due process.

keyVerses.text: Now then, if thou sawest her, tell me under what tree thou sawest them conversing together. He said: Under a mastic tree. And Daniel said: Well hast thou lied against thy own head: for behold the angel of God having received the sentence of him, shall cut thee in two.
keyVerses.why: The trap springs on a detail — separated witnesses inventing independently will disagree on the small things.

questions.question: Why isn't this chapter in Protestant Bibles?
questions.answer: Susanna exists only in the Greek Septuagint additions to Daniel; the Hebrew and Aramaic text of Daniel has twelve chapters. Jerome translated it for the Latin Vulgate (where it is Daniel 13), and Catholic and Orthodox Bibles follow that numbering. Protestant reformers followed the shorter Hebrew canon, so the story dropped out — Luther called the apocrypha 'books not held equal to Scripture, but useful and good to read.'

questions.question: Why do the two trees matter so much?
questions.answer: Daniel separates the witnesses and asks each, independently, under what tree the adultery happened. One says a mastic (a small resinous shrub — too low for the scene described), the other a holm oak (an evergreen). The contradiction proves perjury — and each liar is sentenced to the measure he intended: 'cut thee in two.' Details convict liars.

questions.question: Is Susanna's choice — death over sin — meant as a rule for everyone?
questions.answer: The story presents it as the right choice for her, and the assembly's later praise confirms it. Scripture honors her as it honors the martyrs who refused to lie or bow. It does not teach that every victim of coercion must die; it teaches that some things are worse than death, and that God sees the hidden heart she preserved.

questions.question: Why does the story open with 'wickedness came from Babylon from ancient judges'?
questions.answer: The line (13:5) quotes the Lord's own verdict on the exile's leadership — the corruption is systemic, not incidental. The two elders are not an anomaly but the fruit of an unaccountable judiciary. That framing makes Daniel's reform of the process, not just the verdict, the story's real deliverance.

questions.question: Why does the early church love this story?
questions.answer: It was read in the Easter season — the innocent condemned and vindicated, the false witnesses exposed, 'the innocent blood saved the same day' (13:62) all echo Christ's own trial. Artists painted it for centuries; the scene of Susanna and the elders became one of the most depicted subjects in Western art.

glossary.def: Susanna's husband, the richest and most honored Jew in Babylon.
The mastic — a small shrub-like tree; too low for the scene the elder describes.
The holm oak — a large evergreen; the second elder's contradicting answer.
Elders — the senior men who served as judges and magistrates.
